AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to capping cost sharing for
insulin
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S504

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to capping cost sharing
for insulin

 
PURPOSE:

To reduce the cap on cost sharing for insulin from the current $100 per
insulin prescription per month to $30 per month, in aggregate, for all
insulin drugs.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Sections 1 through 3 of the bill amend various sections of insurance law
which were amended as part DDD of Chapter 56 of the laws of 2020, the
adopted budget, to change the $100 limit on cost sharing for each insu-
lin prescription to a $30 limit per month on cost sharing for all insu-
lin prescriptions.

Section 4 of the bill provides for an effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

An estimated 1.6 million New Yorkers have diabetes and many type 2
diabetics are insulin dependent. Each year there are thousands of hospi-
talizations in NY with a principal diagnosis of diabetes-related compli-
cations including diabetic ketoacidosis.

Type 1 and some Type 2 diabetics depend upon insulin for their very
survival. In 2016, the average person with type 1 diabetes incurred
annual insulin costs of $5,705.00. While some pay less, many others pay
many times this amount. When patients can't afford insulin, which can
cost thousands of dollars even for those who are insured, they resort to
rationing the little medication they can afford. In fact, one study
found that one in four people with type 1 diabetes admitted to not
taking their insulin as prescribed or rationing due to the cost. Compli-
cations from rationing insulin are extreme, leading to amputations,
Diabetic Ketoacidosis, also referred to as DKA, and even death.

As part of the adopted SFY 2020-21 state budget, a cap on cost sharing
was adopted (Part DDD, Chapter 56 of 2020). However, the budget language
capped cost sharing per prescription. Given many diabetics rely on two
or three different types of insulin, they may still have cost sharing of
$300 per month. This legislation changes the $100 cap per prescription
to an aggregate $30 cap on all insulin prescriptions for a given calen-
dar month.

A $30 cap on insulin is also in line with the caps other states are
pursuing and adopting to address access to affordable insulin. For exam-
ple, Utah recently adopted a $30 copay and states such as New Mexico,
Virginia, California, and Connecticut are all in various stages of pass-
ing and adopting copays that range from $25 to $50 per insulin. Addi-
tionally, President Biden signed the Inflation Reduction Act, which
includes a $35 per month out-of-pocket insulin cap for Medicare benefi-
ciaries, beginning January 2023. While New York's new law capping insu-
lin prescription cost sharing at $100 is an important first step, we
must truly make access to insulin affordable and reduce the copay to an
aggregate total of $30 a month.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2022 - S1413 (Rivera) - Passed Senate

2021 - S1413 (Rivera) - Passed Senate

2020 - S8255 (Rivera) - Passed Senate

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

No cost to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately and shall apply to any policy or contract written or renewed
on or after January 1, 2023.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S504A

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to prohibiting cost shar-
ing for insulin

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Sections 1 through 3 of the bill amend various sections of insurance law
which were amended as part DDD of Chapter 56 of the laws of 2020; the
adopted budget, to eliminate any deductible, copayment, coinsurance or
any other cost sharing requirement for insulin drugs.

Section 4 of the bill provides for an effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

An estimated 1.6 million New Yorkers have diabetes and many type 2
diabetics are insulin dependent. Each year there are thousands of hospi-
talizations in NY with a principal diagnosis of diabetes-related compli-
cations including diabetic ketoacidosis.

Type 1 and some Type 2 diabetics depend upon insulin for their very
survival. In 2016, the average person with type 1 diabetes incurred
annual insulin costs of $5,705.00. While some pay less, many others pay
many times this amount. When patients can't afford insulin, which can
cost thousands of dollars even for those who are insured, they resort to
rationing the little medication they can afford. In fact, one study
found that one in four people with type 1 diabetes admitted to not
taking their insulin as prescribed or rationing due to the cost. Compli-
cations from rationing insulin are extreme, leading to amputations,
Diabetic Ketoacidosis, also referred to as DKA, and even death.

As part of the adopted SFY 2020-21 state budget, a cap of $100 on cost
sharing was adopted (Part DDD, Chapter 56 of 2020). However, the budget
language capped cost sharing per prescription. Given many diabetics rely
on two or three different types of insulin, they may still have cost
sharing of $300 per month. This legislation would eliminate any deduct-
ible, copayment, coinsurance or any other cost sharing requirement for
insulin drugs.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2023 - S504 (Rivera) - Passed Senate

2022 - S1413 (Rivera) - Passed Senate

2021 - S1413 (Rivera) - Passed Senate

2020 - S8255 (Rivera) - Passed Senate

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

No cost to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately and shall apply to any policy or contract written or renewed
on or after January 1, 2023.

summary: Prohibits cost sharing for insulin; provides that an insured shall not be subject to a deductible, copayment, coinsurance or any other cost sharing requirement for the purchase of insulin.
